issues.legal_issue: A party that applies for a licence and is refused it when a competing applicant receives renewal of the same licence is a person aggrieved and may appeal the licensing authority’s order.
material_facts: The owners applied for the licence while the tenant applied to renew the same licence.
The licensing authority renewed the tenant’s licence and rejected the owners’ application.
The owners appealed that order to the Board of Revenue.
issues.conclusion: The owners were persons aggrieved by the licensing authority’s order and were competent to appeal under section 5(7) of the Act.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 5(7) of the Madras Cinemas (Regulation) Act, 1955, a person aggrieved may appeal. Because the owners sought the same licence and the order granted the competing applicant’s renewal while refusing their application, they were directly aggrieved; the Court found it unnecessary to consider the other provisions invoked on this point.

predicates.administrative_licensing_appeal: A party challenged a licensing authority’s order before the designated appellate authority.
predicates.competing_license_application: The appealing party applied for the same licence that another applicant sought to renew.
predicates.adverse_order_on_own_application: The licensing authority granted the other applicant’s renewal and refused the appealing party’s application.

issues.definition: When a party appeals a licensing order after seeking the same licence and receiving an adverse decision while a competing applicant receives renewal, that party is a person aggrieved.

issues.legal_issue: The rule requiring an applicant to establish lawful possession applies to both the grant and the renewal of a cinema licence.
material_facts: The tenant sought renewal of an existing cinema licence.
The relevant rule appeared in the general part of the rules governing licences.
The Act barred the licensing authority from granting a licence unless satisfied that the rules had been substantially complied with.
issues.conclusion: Rule 13 applies to renewal as well as to the grant of a licence.
issues.legal_principle: Rule 13 appears in Part I-A of the Madras Cinemas (Regulation) Rules, 1957, under the heading “General.” Section 5(2)(a) of the Madras Cinemas (Regulation) Act, 1955 requires substantial compliance with the rules before a licence is granted. The Court found no basis for distinguishing a grant from a renewal for this purpose.

predicates.cinema_licensing_proceeding: An applicant sought a licence governed by rules regulating cinema licensing.
predicates.application_seeks_renewal: The applicant asked the licensing authority to renew an existing licence.

issues.definition: In a cinema licensing proceeding, an application to renew an existing licence is governed by the applicable licensing rule.

issues.legal_issue: A non-statutory tenant whose lease has expired and who remains in possession against the landlord’s wishes is not in lawful possession for the purpose of establishing eligibility for a licence as a non-owner.
material_facts: The applicant was a tenant under a fixed-term lease of the premises and the cinema equipment.
The lease expired, required the tenant to return the property, and the landlord had given notice requiring its return.
The landlord did not assent to the tenant’s continued possession and applied for the licence itself.
The applicant’s only documentary evidence of possession was the expired lease.
The tenancy was not protected by rent-control legislation.
The applicant sought to rely on the protection against forcible dispossession, but the Court found that this protection did not establish lawful possession.
issues.conclusion: The tenant’s possession after expiry of the lease was not lawful possession under Rule 13, and the Board of Revenue was right to set aside the renewal.
issues.legal_principle: Under the second part of Rule 13 of the Madras Cinemas (Regulation) Rules, 1957, a non-owner must produce documentary evidence, to the licensing authority’s satisfaction, of lawful possession. Lawful possession requires a foundation in a legal right to possess and cannot be equated with juridical possession that merely protects a person against forcible dispossession. Sections 9 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877, and 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, prohibit dispossession without due process but do not make continued possession after expiry of a lease lawful. The Court also relied on the lease obligation to return the property and section 108(q) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, which requires a lessee, on determination of the lease, to put the lessor in possession. Section 5(1) of the 1955 Act makes the public interest relevant to licensing. The Court distinguished Lalu Yeshwant Singh v. Rao Jagdish Singh, which concerned juridical possession and did not decide whether such possession was lawful for this licensing rule; it also referred to K. K. Verma v. Naraindas Malkani, Yar Mohammad v. Lakshmi Das, Midnapur Zamindary Company Ltd. v. Naresh Narayan Roy, and C. Bhavarlal v. Ballay Gounder.

rule.if: nonowner_cinema_license_application and lease_expired and landlord_withheld_consent and no_statutory_tenancy_protection

predicates.nonowner_cinema_license_application: An applicant who did not own the site, building, or equipment sought a cinema licence and had to establish lawful possession.
predicates.lease_expired: The applicant’s fixed-term lease of the property had ended.
predicates.landlord_withheld_consent: The landlord required return of the property and did not agree to the applicant remaining in possession.
predicates.no_statutory_tenancy_protection: No applicable tenancy law protected the applicant’s continued possession against eviction through lawful process.

issues.definition: When a non-owner seeks a cinema licence after the lease has ended, the landlord opposes continued possession, and no tenancy law protects that possession, the continued possession is not lawful for licensing purposes.

issues.legal_issue: The High Court should not interfere under Article 226 with an appellate authority’s order when that order contains no manifest error of law.
material_facts: The Board of Revenue set aside the licensing authority’s renewal order after finding that the tenant was not in lawful possession.
A single Judge dismissed the tenant’s writ petition and declined to disturb the Board’s order.
A Division Bench reversed the single Judge by interpreting the tenant’s post-lease possession as lawful.
The Supreme Court found the Board’s order correct and found no manifest error of law in it.
issues.conclusion: There was no scope for interference under Article 226; the Division Bench’s decision was set aside and the writ petition stood dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the limits on judicial review under Article 226: absent a manifest error of law in the appellate authority’s order, the High Court had no basis to interfere. The Court held that the Board of Revenue was right to intervene and that the Division Bench had misinterpreted Rule 13.

predicates.constitutional_writ_challenge_to_appella: A party asked a High Court to set aside an order made by an administrative appellate authority.
predicates.appellate_order_has_no_manifest_error_of: The appellate authority’s order contains no manifest error of law.

issues.definition: When a party challenges an administrative appellate order by constitutional writ and that order contains no manifest error of law, High Court interference is unwarranted.
